why: within 3 days of Copom decision (3-4 Nov) (2026-11-04)

questions.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%, and 0% as a lower bound on the wider count). S&P usually moves the outlook to negative before it cuts, so I start near zero and allow a small tail for an off-pattern cut.

factors.text: The reference class is clean on this point. S&P has not cut any of these six EU sovereigns straight from a stable outlook since 2014. The normal path is an outlook change first, and an outlook change alone resolves NO. This is the main reason I sit well below the market.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse, which gives S&P cover to act. HCFP calls the 1.0% growth forecast optimistic and sees debt rising toward about 122%. Budget adoption by 31 December is close to a coin flip (50.5% and 49%). Marine Le Pen is priced at 41.1% to win in 2027. The OAT-Bund spread widened from 81.5bp to 96.7bp on the monthly series. This mostly argues for a negative outlook, but it keeps a direct cut possible.

Where the crowd may share an error: the 26.5% Polymarket price trades on thin volume (7345). The 31% Kalshi contract covers any agency through year-end, so it is wider than this question. Both seem to treat a bad fiscal story as if it meant an S&P cut on 27 Nov, and skip the outlook-first habit. The spread series is a degraded monthly average, and no gauge here is tested as a lead on rating actions.

questions.what_would_change_view: Any of these before 27 Nov would push me up toward the market: the government falls on a censure motion, PLF 2027 is rejected at first reading so a special law becomes the base case, or the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. A confirmation that S&P's current outlook is already negative, not stable, would also break the reference class. A quiet first reading with the revenue part passed would push me toward affirm_stable.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The 'stable outlook going in' premise could be wrong, or S&P could decide that political paralysis before the 2027 election justifies an off-pattern cut. In either case the 0% reference class does not apply and the market's roughly one-in-four is closer to right.
questions.title: S&P review of France, 27 Nov 2026

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I give more weight to the subset since France lost its majority in 2022. The page shows that subset separately but does not quote it. Its branch notes say the 2024 and 2025 cycles both ended with a special law. The most relevant starting point is therefore roughly a coin flip for a minority government, well below 90.5%.

factors.text: Structural: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution. The last two budget cycles both missed 31 December and ended with a special law, the 2024 and 2025 pattern noted on the scenario page. The full-sample base rate of 90.5% mostly comes from years with a majority.

This budget is politically harder than usual. It has about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of the civil-service pay index. It lands just before the spring 2027 presidential race, in which Le Pen has launched her campaign and is priced at 41.1%. Opposition parties gain little from letting it pass, and a 49.3 invites a censure vote.

The government has tools to force it through. Kalshi prices use of Article 49.3 on the budget in 2026 at 66%. The Article 47 deadline of 10 December also opens a never-used ordinance route. This keeps the chance of adoption well above zero, provided the government survives.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if PS or LR publicly commit not to censure a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if a censure motion gathers PS votes, if the revenue part fails at first reading in November, or if the government signals a special law as in 2024 and 2025.
questions.most_likely_wrong: Prediction markets at 50.5% and 49% may be right. The government may have secured a quiet non-censure deal, like the one that eventually passed the 2026 budget, and simply land it before Christmas this time, given the reputational cost of a third consecutive special law. My pre-election pessimism could then be overdone. The market signals themselves carry little tested evidence, and the official-optimism gauge is untested.
questions.title: France 2027 budget and the Article 47 deadline

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed probability for an RN win. Its reference class says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 presidential run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp. That only helps once final polls exist, and the snapshot holds no polls six months out. As a last resort I start from market prices: on Polymarket, Le Pen at 41.1% plus Bardella at 1.7%; on Kalshi, Le Pen at 45% plus Bardella at 1.4%. Together that puts the RN candidate in the low-to-mid 40s.

factors.text: Markets price the RN candidate highest among single candidates. Le Pen has formally launched her campaign, and headlines are framing the race as hers to lose. That keeps the starting point near the market level. Note that the market splits RN odds between Le Pen and Bardella as though her ineligibility case were mostly settled; the question counts either name, so that split does not change the YES side.

The centre-right side is split across Lisnard at 19.6%, Philippe at 14.5%, Lagarde at 4.2% and others, and together they are close to the RN total. A run-off is usually a two-way race in which non-RN voters consolidate, and the signposts say that consolidation (withdrawals, sponsorship totals in March 2027) has not happened yet. I shade slightly below the market because fragmented anti-RN odds tend to understate the eventual run-off opponent.

The crowd's main gauge carries little evidential weight. The poll-versus-prediction-market gap is badged tested_no_lead, and prediction-market series in general are tested_no_lead. These markets have high volume but are untested as forecasters this far out. Fiscal strain could still feed the anti-incumbent vote: HCFP expects debt to rise toward about 122% of GDP and sees the 2029 deficit target as very unlikely to be met.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if second-round polls against the leading centre-right candidate show RN ahead by more than the 5.78 pp historical poll error, or if the centre-right stays split into March 2027. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates (the others withdraw) and run-off polls show RN behind. A ruling that keeps Le Pen off the ballot would matter only if Bardella polled weaker than her.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be underrating RN. The old pattern of anti-RN voters uniting in the run-off may have weakened enough, under fiscal austerity and a polarised climate, that the market's low-to-mid 40s is too low rather than too high.
questions.title: France 2027 presidential election

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. My starting point is a judgement-based reference class: Brazil's recent self-set target cuts. The page lists two, in July 2015 and April 2024. Both came mid-year or with the April budget-guidelines bill, not in the first quarter of a year. On that basis a formal change inside a window ending 31 March is less likely than not, and I start around two-thirds YES before the evidence below.

factors.text: The government's own 2027 budget bill claims the target is met. It shows a surplus of R$83.4 billion (0.6% of GDP) counted for the target, against the R$73.2 billion target. A government that says it complies has little reason to send a bill cutting the target before the first bimonthly report around 22 March. The window also closes only about three months into the new term, and the 2015 and 2024 precedents came in July and April.

Independent numbers sit far below the target. The Focus 2027 primary-balance median is -0.4% of GDP, below even the lower tolerance bound; the most optimistic respondent is at 0.5. IFI sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP and about R$40 billion of unbudgeted commitments. In IFI's scenario about R$35.7 billion of discretionary spending would have to be frozen. That gap makes a target cut, or a rule change via the still-pending budget-guidelines bill in December, a live option. It could arrive before March.

Bond markets repriced hard after Lula's run-off win. The 10y rose 255bp on day 1. In the week to 30 Oct the DI Jan-29 proxy rose 212bp and the longest fixed-rate Tesouro bond rose 233bp, to 15.29%. Investors are clearly pricing looser fiscal policy. These are price signals rather than tested forecasts: the Tesouro series is badged untested and the DI proxy is degraded. I give them some weight, not much.

questions.what_would_change_view: Toward NO: a PLN changing the 2027 target attached to the December budget-guidelines or budget (PLOA) vote; ministers publicly questioning the 0.5% target; a January finance minister who talks of rewriting LC 200/2023. Toward YES: the PLOA voted around 17 Dec without new exclusions, and a new finance minister who commits to the framework. The 20 Nov bimonthly report (RARDP) and its freeze size are an early read on intent.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The 2027 target may not yet be locked in, because the budget-guidelines bill is still pending. Congress or the government could lower the target there in December, quietly and before the new term even starts. That would turn my modal 'kept on paper' branch into NO well before the March report. The crowd's shared error may run the other way: markets price an immediate loosening of the actual fiscal path, but this question resolves on formal paperwork. A government can miss the target on Focus and IFI numbers for months without sending a bill to change it.
questions.title: Brazil 2027: fiscal-framework credibility

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page's computed base rate (final-poll leader won 3 of 3 Mexican midterms; RMS poll error 4.12 pp) tells us who leads, not whether the coalition clears 334 of 500 seats. It does not answer this question directly. So I start from the same page's qualitative note: at the most recent midterm in the class, 2021, the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. That is a starting point below even odds for a supermajority, with a simple majority as the default outcome.

factors.text: Midterm erosion is the default pattern. In 2021, the last midterm in em-macro's reference class, the governing coalition held a majority but lost two-thirds. Two-thirds needs both a high vote share (the page's signpost is above 55%) and favourable over-representation rulings from the INE, so several things must go right at once.

Polls have underestimated this coalition's strength before. In 2024 Sheinbaum led by 17pp and won by 33pp, and the congressional supermajority surprised markets badly. The primer names supermajorities that a two-candidate poll margin cannot capture as a known place where consensus errs. That keeps the YES tail fatter than a simple midterm-erosion story implies.

The crowd sees Morena as dominant: 87.5% on Polymarket and 86% on Kalshi that it wins the most seats, with PAN at 7.8%. That argues against the coalition losing its majority. But these are related-only contracts that say nothing about the 334-seat line, and prediction-market series carry a tested_no_lead badge, so I give them little weight beyond the low lose_majority branch.

questions.what_would_change_view: Mid-2027 polls putting the coalition's combined vote above 55% would push me toward or above even odds. Below 45% would raise lose_majority. An INE ruling that tightens or loosens the coalition over-representation rules (the 2024 dispute) would move the seat maths directly. Candidate registration and precampaigns in January 2027 will be the first hard read on alliance arrangements in key districts.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be anchoring too much on midterm erosion. If the coalition repeats its 2024 pattern of beating polls, and the seat allocation again rewards the alliance, two-thirds could be the more likely outcome. The market's dominance pricing would then be the better guide, and I would be underweighting a known polling blind spot that I flagged myself.
questions.title: Mexico midterms, 6 Jun 2027

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle, and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. As a last resort I start from market prices on the 2026 review. Those markets put a 16-year extension in 2026 at 8% (pm:2761052) and 12% (ks:KXUSMCAOUTCOMES-27-16Y), against 13% for a US withdrawal notice. They resolve on a different, earlier window, and the 2026 review has already passed without an extension.

factors.text: The first chance to extend has already been missed. The 2026 review ended without a 16-year extension, which is why annual joint reviews now apply. A US administration that passed on extending once has shown it prefers the leverage of a recurring review over locking in a long term.

USTR is actively using the agreement's enforcement tools against Mexico, such as the labour-rights case at Madobox. In the same week it signed a memorandum of understanding with Mexico, so engagement continues. This looks like managing the deal case by case, which fits continued annual reviews better than a clean written extension from all three countries.

Markets give a revised trilateral deal some chance: 24% for 2026 (ks:KXUSMCAOUTCOMES-27-TRI). A renegotiated text could be paired with an extension, which keeps YES from being remote. But these are thin, low-volume contracts, and prediction-market gauges are badged tested_no_lead, so I give them little weight.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's 2027 public consultation (placeholder date around 1 Feb 2027) or its report recommends extension, or if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut below 10%; both are signposts on the scenario page. I would move down if the US proposes separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, or officials describe withdrawal as leverage. A firm date for the next bilateral round (the 30 Nov placeholder) would also help.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The US could decide it has extracted enough concessions, through a revised deal or side agreements, and grant the written extension at the 1 Jul 2027 review to claim a win. Under that reading the 2026 miss was a negotiating pause, not a preference for annual reviews. The crowd and I may both be anchoring too heavily on the 2026 outcome. There is also a shared blind spot in the other direction: the peso is calm at 18.7592 and leveraged funds are long the peso at the 79.5th percentile (a tested_no_lead gauge). That suggests little tail risk is priced, and an off-calendar US trade announcement could change the picture faster than the scheduled review.
questions.title: USMCA annual review, 1 Jul 2027

why_it_matters.text: Long-dated Brazilian bonds have repriced sharply since the 25 Oct run-off. The longest fixed-rate Tesouro bond rose from 12.96% to 15.29% in a week, and the DI Jan-29 proxy rose from 12.83% to 14.95%. The DI Jan-27 proxy moved only to 13.54%, so this is mainly a long-end fiscal risk premium, not near-term rate hikes. In em-macro's hold-out, bond moves after elections tended to continue rather than reverse. Caveat: these DI figures are Tesouro LTN proxies, not the DI curve itself.

The long inflation-linked (IPCA+) yield rose less than the fixed-rate one, from 6.56% to 7.48%. Part of the repricing is therefore higher inflation compensation. That fits the Focus 2027 IPCA median of 4.76%, up 0.545 point in three months and well above the 3.6% assumed in the 2027 budget bill.

The real keeps weakening: USD/BRL PTAX reached 5.4935 on 3 Nov, up 1.33% since 30 Oct and 2.98% on the week. em-macro's hold-out found that election currency moves continued rather than reversed. Fading the day-1 move lost money, including on Brazil's 2022 run-off, so there is no tested reason to expect a rebound.

The fiscal gap is the core of the story. The 2027 budget bill claims a surplus counted for the target of 0.6% of GDP, against the 0.5% target. The Senate's IFI sees only R$0.9 billion and says R$35.7 billion of spending would need freezing. Focus respondents expect a 2027 primary balance of -0.4% of GDP. The wider the gap, the more the long end and the real depend on December's budget vote and January's policy choices.

Today's Copom matters for the real because forecasters disagree unusually widely. Dispersion on the Selic call is at the 87.5th percentile, with a median of 13.5% against the current 13.75%. In Brazil, that kind of dispersion has tested as a lead for the decision missing the survey median, though not for the size of the move. In-sample, a 25bp surprise was worth about 0.4–0.7% on the real, but rate-surprise regressions added almost nothing out of sample.

The interest-rate gap still favours the real: the Selic is 13.75% against a US effective fed funds rate of 3.88%. Leveraged funds were only mildly long the real (67.3rd percentile on 27 Oct), and that gauge has no tested lead. So positioning neither cushions nor threatens the currency in any reliable way.

watch.what_to_watch: Hold at 13.75% or a cut to the Focus median of 13.5%? Polymarket gives a 25bp cut only 10.5%, so the survey and the market disagree. With dispersion this high, a miss against the survey median is the tested risk. Read the statement for how the Copom treats the post-election jump in long yields, the weaker real and fiscal risk.

The first survey after Copom. Watch the year-end Selic medians (13.5% for 2026, 12.5% for 2027, which already rose 0.5 point in three months) and whether the 2027 IPCA median climbs above 4.76% as the weaker real feeds through.
The 2027 primary-balance median, now -0.4% of GDP. Any further fall below the 0.5% target is a signpost for the 'target cut' branch. Also check whether dispersion (sd 0.297) widens.

Does the government enlarge the 2026 spending freeze, or revise revenue and spending forecasts toward IFI's view of a 2026 primary deficit of 0.5% of GDP (Focus median -0.49%)? Watch for new items carved out of the spending limit, and any hint that the 2027 assumptions of 2.5% growth and 3.6% inflation will be revised toward Focus.

Whether 2027 inflation and Selic expectations keep drifting up. A rising 2027 Selic median alongside a falling 2027 GDP median (now 1.2%) would mean the market sees fiscal slippage being paid for with tighter money.
The Selic call for the 9 Dec Copom and its dispersion, as the budget (PLOA) vote approaches around 17 Dec. A high-dispersion reading would again flag the risk of a miss against the survey median.

risks.text: The fiscal framework is loosened: the 2027 target is cut or the spending rule changed. The scenario's Nov 2024 analog moved the DI Jan-29 proxy up 112bp and USD/BRL up 4.39% in three trading days. Signposts are a bill to change the target or LC 200/2023, and the Focus 2027 primary median falling further below target.

A Copom surprise in either direction. A cut into a weakening real and rising long yields could read as dovish under fiscal strain and hurt the currency. An unexpectedly hawkish signal could steepen pain at the front end. High survey dispersion makes a miss against the median more likely.

The post-election selloff extends instead of reversing. em-macro's hold-out found election currency moves continued, and bond moves continued in-sample. The run-off day-1 moves (10y +255bp, real -8.4% on PTAX) may not be the end of it.

Hidden fiscal pressure outside the headline target. IFI flags off-budget credit and fund operations, about R$40 billion of unbudgeted commitments, and a R$104.8 billion gap between its result projection and the bill's. The consumption-tax transition adds a R$33.8 billion fund payment.
A global risk-off move hits high-carry currencies. The VIX rose to 21.15, up 15.01% in a week, while the US 10-year sits at 4.91%.

consensus.view: Surveys still expect easing: the Focus median for today's Copom is 13.5%, a 25bp cut from 13.75%, with year-end medians of 13.5% for 2026 and 12.5% for 2027. Prediction markets disagree on today: Polymarket gives a 25bp cut only 10.5%, and Kalshi's most likely count of 2026 cuts is exactly 5 at 62% (down 6 points). On fiscal policy, the consensus is that the 0.5% 2027 target will be missed. The Focus median is -0.4% of GDP, IFI projects a potential 1.0% deficit, and the fixed-rate curve has added well over 200bp at the long end in a week while the real weakened to 5.4935.

BR.might_be_wrong: The shared error may be treating 'the target is missed' as the same thing as 'the framework is abandoned'. Focus, IFI and the bond market all point at a miss. But the rule counts the result after legal deductions, which is how the budget bill reaches 0.6% of GDP, and the target has a 0.25-point tolerance band. Hitting the target on paper through exclusions and one-offs still counts as the target being kept in the scenario. The 212bp rise in the DI Jan-29 proxy is already larger than the 112bp of the Nov 2024 'target cut' analog, so a merely muddled 'kept on paper' outcome could disappoint bond bears. The counterweights are that no version of em-macro's mispricing signal beat 'no change' out of sample, and post-election bond moves tended to continue. 'Overpriced' is a judgement, not a tested edge. On Copom, the survey median (cut) and Polymarket (hold) cannot both be right, and high dispersion warns that the survey median is the likelier one to miss.

why_it_matters.text: The peso still pays a wide interest margin: Banxico's rate is 6.5% against a US federal funds rate of 3.88%. That margin is the main reason investors hold pesos. Betting odds on a 25bp cut on 5 Nov jumped to 24.9% from 13.6%, and the odds of no change fell to 73.5%. Any sign the margin will shrink faster matters more for the peso than the cut itself. USD/MXN stands at 18.7592, 0.57% weaker for the peso over the week, while the broad dollar rose only 0.28%.

Mexican 10-year yields have been the most reliable responders to rate surprises in em-macro's early sample, rising 0.50bp per bp of hawkish surprise. In the 2022-26 hold-out, however, rate-surprise regressions added almost nothing, and decisions were quieter than before. Treat a Banxico surprise as a modest bond event, not a regime change. The 10-year auction yield last printed 9.25%, down 10bp, helped by a US 10-year that eased to 4.91%.

The 2027 budget package loosens consolidation. It targets a broad deficit of 3.9% of GDP against the 3.5% planned in April, and it still includes Pemex capital contributions of 81.1 billion pesos. México Evalúa says this does not stabilise debt. Because index eligibility depends on the middle of the three agency ratings, fiscal slippage is the slow-burning risk for Mbonos. KBRA's affirmation at BBB stable on 30 Oct buys time but is not the agency that matters most.

The 28-day interbank rate (TIIE) rose 15.1bp in a week to 6.9167% while the policy rate stayed at 6.5%. Short-term peso funding got dearer just as betting markets moved toward a cut. That mismatch should resolve after 5 Nov, one way or the other.

US trade moves are the biggest driver of large peso swings and rarely follow the calendar. USTR filed a new labour-rights case (Madobox) on 2 Nov alongside a separate agreement at another plant. Kalshi prices a US withdrawal notice from USMCA in 2026 at 13%, and Polymarket gives an extension in 2026 only 8%.

watch.what_to_watch: Markets lean to a hold at 6.5% (73.5%) with a cut priced at 24.9%. Watch three things: the decision, whether the vote is split, and whether the statement keeps the door open to cuts. A cut with dovish guidance would test the carry case for the peso. A hold that signals the easing is over would support it. The hold-out evidence says decision-day moves are usually small, so judge it by the peso and 10-year over several days, not the first hour.

Watch whether the Chamber approves the spending budget on time. Then check whether it keeps the 3.9% of GDP broad-deficit path and the 81.1 billion pesos of Pemex support, or adds spending. Upward changes to Pemex transfers or unfunded spending would weaken the case behind the deficit path and matter for ratings.
watch.event: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)

watch.what_to_watch: No date has been announced yet; the first signal is whether USTR sets one. Watch for new labour-rights cases like Madobox, any tariff announcement, and whether US officials frame withdrawal as leverage. A surprise announcement outside the round is more likely to move the peso than the round itself.
watch.event: USMCA: US-Mexico bilateral round (next round not announced)

watch.what_to_watch: Check whether the 2026 year-end policy-rate median stays at 6.5% (range 6.25 to 6.75) after the 5 Nov decision. Also watch whether the 2027 broad-balance median drifts from -3.7%, and whether 2027 growth expectations (1.83%) fall toward the low end of the government's 1.5% to 2.5% range.

risks.text: An unscheduled US trade action, such as tariffs or a USMCA withdrawal threat, hits the peso hard and fast. In the 2024 election the peso fell 3.5% on day 1 and 7.2% by day 5, and hold-out FX moves continued rather than reversed.

Fiscal slippage repeats. IMEF reports the 2025 broad deficit at 4.8% against 3.9% planned. Pemex remains a drain, with first-half 2026 losses of 28 billion pesos and debt above US$77 billion. A repeat would push the rating that sets index eligibility closer to the edge.

A faster easing path narrows the interest margin over the US while leveraged funds are already long pesos (24.5% of open interest, 79.5th percentile). Positioning has no tested predictive value, so this is a risk to the size of any move, not a forecast of its direction.
Global risk appetite turns. The VIX rose to 21.15 over the week, and carry currencies like the peso tend to suffer first when volatility climbs.

consensus.view: Surveys and markets expect a steady Mexico. Economists see the policy rate at 6.5% at end-2026 and end-2027, inflation of 3.88% this year and 3.85% next, and growth of 1.5% then 1.83%. Betting markets favour a hold on 5 Nov (73.5%). The survey's median deficit for 2026 is 3.9% of GDP, the same figure the government initially planned. Markets see USMCA staying in annual-review limbo, with extension in 2026 at 8% and a US withdrawal notice at 13%. Leveraged funds hold a large long-peso position.

MX.might_be_wrong: The shared error is likely fiscal anchoring. The economists' 2026 deficit median (3.9%) sits on the government's original plan, yet IMEF reports 2025 ended at 4.8% against a 3.9% plan. The official-optimism gauge is untested, so nobody has checked whether surveys systematically lag official misses (badge:d). A second shared assumption is that trade risk is scheduled around the July 2027 review, when the primer and the 2024 episode warn that US decisions arrive off-calendar. On rates, the crowd is less settled than the survey suggests: cut odds nearly doubled in a day while the 28-day interbank rate rose 15.1bp, so expectations for the 5 Nov decision are moving in opposite directions. The long-peso positioning makes an unwind sharper if any of these turns, though that gauge carries no tested signal (badge:e).

why_it_matters.text: The French 10-year spread over Germany widened sharply before the latest budget and rating news. The monthly average rose from 81.5bp in August to 96.7bp in September, and the French 10-year averaged 4.44% against 4.0%. The Bund was 3.38% on 2026-10-30. These are ECB monthly averages that can be up to five weeks old, so any October or November move is not yet visible. The series is also untested as a signal.

The 2027 budget is the main driver of the spread. The bills carry about 54 billion euros of consolidation and aim to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5.0% in 2027. The fiscal watchdog (HCFP) calls the 1.0% growth assumption optimistic. It says the plan works only if every measure passes, and it sees debt rising toward about 122% of GDP. A minority government must pass all of this, likely through Article 49.3, which invites a censure vote.

S&P reviews France on 27 November. The scenario page's own guesses for the spread are about -2bp for a plain affirmation, +4bp for a move to a negative outlook, and about 12.3bp (range 9.69 to 14.92) for a cut to A. A one-notch S&P cut is unlikely to trigger forced selling, because France would still keep a AA-category rating: Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October. That Moody's rating is the one reserve managers' thresholds hinge on.

The 2027 presidential race is already a bond story. Polymarket gives Marine Le Pen 41.1% and Kalshi 45%. The closest analog is the June 2024 dissolution, when an RN majority became possible: the spread widened about 17bp in monthly averages. That pressure can build long before the April 2027 vote.

France has no currency of its own, so French stress shows up in the spread to Germany rather than in the euro. EUR/USD was 1.1199 on 2026-10-23, down only 0.28% on the week (an untested series). The ECB's backstop (TPI) is conditional on fiscal compliance, so a failed budget weakens the safety net for French bonds more than it moves the euro.

watch.what_to_watch: Whether S&P keeps France at A+ and, more likely to matter, whether it changes the outlook. Since 2014, S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns that went in with a stable outlook. An outlook change would resolve the 'downgrade' markets NO but could still widen the spread. Before the date, watch three things: whether a censure motion succeeds before 27 November, whether the National Assembly passes the revenue part of PLF 2027 at first reading, and whether the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate above 5.4%. Agencies usually publish after the Friday close, so the market reaction comes the following Monday. Our monthly spread series will not show it until the December average is published.
watch.event: Standard & Poor's sovereign rating review: France

risks.text: The government falls on a censure motion over the budget. Kalshi puts use of Article 49.3 in 2026 at 66%, and each use invites a censure vote. When the Barnier government fell in December 2024, the monthly spread rose 4.7bp, which understates the daily move. The modelled effect of losing seat share is 19.08bp (range 9.0 to 29.16).

Ratings pile up rather than arriving singly. S&P reviews on 27 November and KBRA on 11 December, while Moody's Aa3 already carries a negative outlook. A further step by Moody's would threaten France's last AA-category rating, which matters for some reserve managers.

Growth and the deficit could slip. The government assumes 1.0% growth in 2027, against a consensus of 0.81%. The HCFP says downside risks dominate and that the 2029 target of a deficit below 3% is very unlikely to be met.

Election risk could be priced early. Le Pen is at 41.1% on Polymarket and has launched her campaign, and the 2024 RN analog widened the spread about 17bp. The modelled effect of a more populist government is 12.44bp, but its range includes zero.

We cannot see or forecast this market well. The spread data are monthly and lag by weeks. The em-macro spread-mispricing model did far worse than 'no change' for France (error ratio 1.59 at 3 months): it kept expecting the spread to narrow while it widened through 2024–26.

consensus.view: The three official forecasters (IMF, OECD and European Commission) put France's deficit at 5.11% of GDP in 2026 and 5.2% in 2027, slightly worse than the government's 5.0% path for 2027. They put 2027 growth at 0.81%, below the budget's 1.0%. Prediction markets treat the budget as a coin flip: 50.5% on Polymarket and 49% on Kalshi for promulgation by 31 December. That compares with 19 of 21 past budgets promulgated on time, although the special laws of 2024 and 2025 show how the minority era differs. Kalshi gives 66% to Article 49.3. Markets price a downgrade by Moody's or S&P by 30 November at 26.5%, and any agency in 2026 at 31%. Le Pen is at 41.1%. The bond market had already pushed the spread to 96.7bp by September.

FR.might_be_wrong: The crowd may be making two linked errors. First, the 26.5% price on a downgrade looks high: S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns going in with a stable outlook since 2014. The likelier bad outcome is an outlook change to negative, which those markets resolve NO. A NO could be misread as relief even if the spread widens a little. Second, forecasters and markets may share the government's assumption that the budget's measures will pass. The three official forecasters sit only a few tenths away from the government's numbers, and the 'official optimism gap' gauge is untested. The real tail is therefore a censure-driven special law and a further slide in growth, not the S&P date itself. Treat all of these market prices with caution: the evidence badges mark prediction markets as tested_no_lead and the French spread series as untested. History also argues against betting on a reversal. Models that called the French spread too wide failed out of sample, so 'it has widened enough' is as risky a consensus as 'the downgrade is coming'.

why_it_matters.text: Gold fell 3.06% over the week to 3949.8 even though its usual supports moved its way. The US 10-year real yield (the inflation-adjusted return on Treasuries, gold's main rival) fell 6bp to 2.60%. The broad dollar rose only 0.28%. So last week's drop was not a rates-or-dollar story. The clearest match is the Geopolitical Risk index, which fell from 165.628 to 97.668 as a fear premium came out of the price.

Silver fell 7.85% over the week to 50.03, more than twice gold's drop. When silver falls much harder than gold, it usually means speculative, leveraged money was leaving precious metals, not that central banks or long-term holders changed their minds. Both metals bounced on 2 November: gold rose 1.31% and silver 1.9%.

For US bonds, the 2-year yield of 4.56% sits above the Fed funds upper limit of 4.0% and the effective rate of 3.88%. Read plainly, the bond market is not pricing a run of Fed cuts. The 10-year at 4.94% also leaves a high real yield of 2.60%. That is a costly backdrop for an asset like gold that pays no interest, and it caps how far gold can rise on rate hopes alone.

The dollar is not the problem for gold right now. The broad index was 121.6656 and barely moved on the day, and EUR/USD was steady at 1.1163. A clear dollar move after the midterms would be a new force rather than a continuation of one.

Official buying, the slow-moving floor under gold, is easing. IMF-reporting central banks bought a net 34.66 tonnes in September, down from 45.76 tonnes in August. They are still buying, but less, so dips have a little less official support.

watch.what_to_watch: Which party controls the House and the Senate. Then check how the 10-year real yield (now 2.60%) and the broad dollar (now 121.6656) react over the following days, rather than gold's first-hour move. A split Congress usually means less new fiscal spending, which would lean real yields lower and help gold modestly. A result that points to larger deficits could push long yields up from 4.94% and weigh on gold. The snapshot's only market hints are combination bets that bundle a Democratic Senate with unrelated events (Polymarket at 43.0%, Kalshi at 29.0%), so they cannot isolate the US outcome. Also check whether the Geopolitical Risk index keeps rising from 97.668, since that, not the election, drove last week.

risks.text: The geopolitical premium can swing back fast in either direction. The index jumped from 77.638 to 97.668 in a single day after falling from 165.628. Gold's next weekly move may track this index more than anything in Washington.

Real yields may stop falling. If the midterm result or the 9 December FOMC projections confirm that rates stay near current levels (2-year at 4.56% against a 4.0% upper limit), the 2.60% real yield would keep holding gold back. A hawkish signal at that meeting would cut against gold.

Selling by speculative holders may not be finished. Silver's 7.85% weekly fall shows leveraged money leaving, and slower central-bank buying (34.66 tonnes in September, down from 45.76 in August) offers a thinner cushion if that selling resumes.

Volatility is rising. The VIX rose 2.22 points to 19.42, and emerging-market stress is visible: the Brazilian real fell 7.61% over the week. In a dash for cash, gold can be sold to cover losses elsewhere before it acts as a safe haven.

consensus.view: There is no survey of gold forecasts in the snapshot, so 'consensus' here means models and market prices. The frozen gold-events model expects a small rebound over five days: gold +0.47% and silver +1.02%. It has been scored on 0 weeks out of sample, so it is untested. Bond pricing is the firmer signal. The 2-year at 4.56% above the 4.0% Fed upper limit implies no near-term easing cycle, while the 10-year real yield edged down to 2.60%. The market treats today's midterms and the 9 December FOMC as the next catalysts, and the bounce of 1.31% on 2 November suggests buyers see last week's 3.06% fall as overdone.

GOLD.might_be_wrong: The shared assumption is that gold trades off US real yields, the dollar and the Fed, so the midterms and the FOMC are what matter. Last week contradicts that. Real yields fell 6bp and the dollar rose only 0.28%, yet gold fell 3.06% and silver 7.85%, while the Geopolitical Risk index nearly halved from 165.628. If the fear premium and speculative positioning are now the main drivers, the midterm reaction could be smaller than people expect, and the next big move could come from a geopolitical headline instead. The model's +0.47% call is built on last week's changes in those same drivers and has no out-of-sample record, so it is no tiebreaker. My confidence is low to moderate. The most likely way I am wrong is a clear midterm result that moves the 10-year real yield sharply, putting the rates channel back in charge.
